title: The Morpho instance splits Curator and Guardian roles behind a 240-hour timelock
content:
The Morpho USDT instance publishes exactly two role addresses — a `Curator Role Address` (A.6.1.1.1.2.6.1.4.3.1.1.4.2.1) and a `Guardian Role Address` (.4.2.2) — plus a bare `Timelock: 240 hours (10 days)` (.4.3).

The three parameters only make sense together. The Curator proposes changes to the vault's market allocation; the timelock delays them; the Guardian can cancel during the delay. Neither role alone can act unilaterally against depositors: the Curator's power is slowed, the Guardian's power is purely negative.

Ten days is a deliberately long window, and it is chosen against a human constraint rather than a technical one. It must exceed the time for a compromise to be *noticed* — including across weekends, holidays and timezone gaps — because the Guardian is presumably a human-operated key. A 24-hour timelock protects against nothing an attacker cannot wait out unobserved.

The cost is symmetric: legitimate risk reductions are also delayed ten days. If a collateral asset starts failing, the Curator cannot pull the allocation faster than the veto window allows. The design therefore accepts slower defence in exchange for guaranteed reviewability — a trade only worth making when the Guardian is genuinely watching.
description: A 10-day delay on Curator actions gives the separately-keyed Guardian a standing window to veto, converting a fast permissioned change into a reviewable one.
